name: Low-Ball Technique
description: Securing agreement to a low initial cost or commitment, then revealing a higher true cost afterward, yields more final compliance than disclosing the full cost upfront -- driven by commitment to the earlier decision, not merely momentum from having already said yes.
design_relevance_note: The mechanism behind drip pricing and post-signup fee reveals -- a known dark-pattern risk in checkout and subscription flows, not a technique to deploy uncritically.
prevalence_note: Named directly in dark-pattern taxonomies (e.g. drip pricing) about as often as in classic persuasion-technique teaching.

findings.description: Inducing an initial low-cost commitment to a behavior and only later revealing that it will cost more produces greater final compliance than disclosing the full cost upfront. The effect was reliable across experiments, mechanistically distinct from the foot-in-the-door effect (per the paper's own Experiment 2), and occurred only when the initial decision was made under a high degree of perceived choice — best explained by commitment rather than competing explanations tested.
findings.source_title: Low-ball procedure for producing compliance: Commitment then cost.
findings.source_venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology

applications.title: StubHub's $10 million FTC settlement for revealing mandatory ticket fees only after the initial price display
applications.description: In April 2026, the US Federal Trade Commission announced that StubHub Holdings, Inc. would pay $10 million in consumer redress to settle charges that it violated the FTC's Rule on Unfair or Deceptive Fees. The FTC alleged that across StubHub's first three ticket-pricing displays, the advertised price did not include mandatory fees, with the total price -- including fulfillment and service fees -- only disclosed later in the purchase flow, after a buyer had already selected specific tickets and progressed toward checkout. This is the digital, incremental-disclosure form of the low-ball mechanism: a low initial price draws in a commitment-forming decision, with the true, higher cost revealed only once the buyer is further along in the process. The violations covered ticket sales between May 12-14, 2025, immediately after the FTC's fee-disclosure rule took effect; StubHub was ordered to provide redress to affected consumers within 90 days.
applications.industry_context: Online ticket resale/marketplace; directly shaped by the FTC's Rule on Unfair or Deceptive Fees, effective May 12, 2025, which now requires upfront total-price disclosure across this industry.
applications.ethical_note: This is not a borderline or debatable case -- it is an adjudicated federal violation, with the FTC's own enforcement action and redress order confirming real consumer harm from the practice. Included here specifically because a real regulatory body's own finding is stronger evidence of manipulative intent/effect than a design commentator's opinion would be.
